satu.name: SATU: Shopping Assistant That Understands
satu.summary: A shopping copilot that treats every product it shows as a commitment rather than a list, and every question it asks as a turn it has to earn.

event.title: Devpost Software Showcase — Staff Picks & Rails

inspiration_intel.the_wedge: They assumed the expensive step (generation, review, data entry) should be priced before it runs.
inspiration_intel.what_it_does: A shopping copilot that treats every product it shows as a commitment rather than a list, and every question it asks as a turn it has to earn.
steal_this: Find the metric practitioners already eyeball, instrument it, and ship the delta. A number turns a vibe into a product.
inspiration_intel.naive_version_vs_this: A demo that needs the user to already know what to type. — then SATU: Shopping Assistant That Understands made the step measurable, gated, or priced instead.
inspiration_intel.reuse_surface: portable to any agent that touches production data

audit.worth_note: Not for the score - for the discipline. A hackathon team published the objective, the metric definitions, the convention for misses, and a baseline row, then made every design decision answerable to it: slate width as a real variable because reciprocal rank is weighted, the dense asset kept in the architecture at weight zero and labelled rejected, one tokenizer shared by index and query so the two can never disagree. It is the rare submission where a reader can recompute the headline number from the page, and the arithmetic closes to four decimals.

numbers_add_up.why: TechnicalScore 0.9672 (SATU) versus 0.1067 (BM25 baseline) (recomputed: recomputed: 0.50*1.000 + 0.30*0.975 + 0.20*clip((11-2.27)/10,0,1) = 0.9671 for SATU, and 0.50*0.125 + 0.30*0.068 + 0.20*clip((11-9.81)/10,0,1) = 0.1067 for the baseline - both rows reproduce the printed figures); HitRate@10 1.000, MRR 0.975, MTTC 2.27 (recomputed: internally consistent with the recomputed objective above; the per-session log was not needed to check the aggregate)

assumptions: you have a catalog with attributes and ratings, since the question value term comes from attribute coverage
you accept a rule-based scored path; the moment a model enters it, the latency and cost claims no longer transfer
the benchmark is the organiser's, so porting it means building your own session harness
clone_cost.estimate: 2-4 days to reproduce the architecture on a catalog you already have; weeks to earn the numbers
clone_cost.why: The scored path is stdlib Python with no model, so the retrieval, ranking, slate shaping and question selection logic is legible in a day and the harness is in the repo. What does not come free is the evaluator and the catalog statistics it leans on - popularity priors, attribute lead lines and rare-phrase evidence are all derived from that specific 50,000-product dump.

audit.what_to_steal: Publish the objective function next to the results, including how failures are counted, so the number can be checked rather than trusted; make the expensive optional component visible at weight zero instead of deleting it, which documents a decision and its cost; use one shared preprocessing function for index and query; and treat 'how many items do I show now' and 'is another question worth a turn' as two explicit, stateful decisions rather than fixed constants.
audit.what_breaks_first: The evaluator's proxy. Optimising 'the session ends when the target appears in the slate' rewards wide early slates and precise question-baiting, which is not the same thing as a shopper being helped; HitRate@10 of 1.000 with 2.27 turns says the target was surfaced, not that the other nine products were good or that the user trusted the answer. Second: state robustness - typed slots, refusals and an exhaustion path are all deterministic logic over a 50k catalog, and the page reports no adversarial or human sessions to show the behaviour selection recovering from a shopper who changes their mind.

prior_art.relation: same genre - an agent pipeline that reports a measured before/after with a cost figure - but the two sit at opposite ends of auditability: Greenlight's numbers are asserted with a stated cost ladder and no harness, SATU's can be recomputed from the formula on the page and its harness is in the linked repository.

both treat the free/default path as a design constraint to be engineered rather than a concession; SketchWish does it with sign-in gates and hard caps against abuse, SATU by keeping the scored path model-free at $0.00 per turn.

sketchwish.name: SketchWish
sketchwish.summary: Turn any photo into a print-ready sketch in seconds, powered by Google Gemini. Built for print-on-demand sellers and gift buyers, live in production today.

inspiration_intel.the_wedge: The team treated the annoying part of the workflow as the product, not the demo.
inspiration_intel.what_it_does: Turn any photo into a print-ready sketch in seconds, powered by Google Gemini. Built for print-on-demand sellers and gift buyers, live in production today.
steal_this: Steal the framing: Marketplace & Matching work inside Money, Commerce & Marketplaces, done as a bounded loop.
inspiration_intel.naive_version_vs_this: A demo that needs the user to already know what to type. — then SketchWish made the step measurable, gated, or priced instead.
inspiration_intel.reuse_surface: portable to any agent that touches production data

audit.worth_note: Not a photo filter but a small company assembled correctly: a cheap vision pass protecting fidelity, an image model doing the rendering, third-party auth, storage, quota and payments so the free tier stays solvent, plus two genuinely hard-won findings - that model deprecation mid-build is an operational risk to design for, and that in-app browsers break Google sign-in so the funnel needs an escape hatch. Most hackathon 'live product' claims are demos; this one names its own margin.

assumptions: you have a Stripe account and a domain, since the product is the checkout
you accept a per-render cost and price the free tier against it
you define 'print-ready' as a test you can fail, or drop the claim
clone_cost.estimate: 1 week for the render pipeline and payment loop, 3 weeks with caps, escapes and analytics wired
clone_cost.why: the models are hosted, and auth, storage, quota and payments are all configuration of existing services

audit.what_to_steal: Engineer the free tier as the abuse surface first: sign-in as the price of a render, a hard generation cap, and an explicit rate limiter as its own component. Then use the cheap model to read and the expensive model to render, so the cost curve, not the vendor's price list, decides how much you can give away.
audit.what_breaks_first: Taste. 'Print-ready' is a per-style judgement, and a paid print-on-demand seller returns goods that merely look like a filter - there is no fidelity metric anywhere in the capture, no style-level acceptance rate, and no human review loop. The single-provider dependency is the other one: they already survived one model retirement mid-build, and the pipeline still has one throat to choke.

prior_art.relation: same commerce logic in another modality: plug into someone else's store and cut a return-logistics cost rather than chase delight
photo in, structured commercially actionable output out - same trust problem, resolved with an estimate instead of an artwork
also sells speed-to-artifact to solo sellers; this one owns the production concern the others skip

carbender.name: Carbender
carbender.summary: A tool for identifying damaged car parts and estimating repair costs. Computer vision turns photos into organized OEM part lists with real-market price reports.

inspiration_intel.the_wedge: They assumed the expensive step (generation, review, data entry) should be priced before it runs.
inspiration_intel.what_it_does: A tool for identifying damaged car parts and estimating repair costs. Computer vision turns photos into organized OEM part lists with real-market price reports.
steal_this: Steal the framing: Retail & Conversion work inside Money, Commerce & Marketplaces, done as a bounded loop.
inspiration_intel.naive_version_vs_this: A demo that needs the user to already know what to type. — then Carbender made the step measurable, gated, or priced instead.
inspiration_intel.reuse_surface: portable to any product whose users hate forms

audit.worth_note: The audience is specific and it pays: people bidding on salvage lots, body shops and mechanics, for whom a photo-to-parts-list-with-prices replaces a guess made in a ten-minute walk-around. Within that audience the wedge is real and better than the obvious alternative, because the two things a human estimator cannot do at an auction - check a 700,000-row OEM catalog and price parts across a jurisdiction boundary - are exactly what the build automates, and the Loss Ratio turns a pile of numbers into the one decision the buyer came with. What keeps it niche rather than strong is that the mechanism does not outlive the project: vision plus grounded pricing plus a published decision ratio is a well-executed instance of a pattern that will be repeated, and the moat is the catalog, not the method. No accuracy figure anywhere means a buyer inherits the author's confidence rather than a measured one - which the page at least admits is the wrong thing to hand over, hence the scarcity banners.

assumptions: a parts catalog with per-model-year coverage, or an accepted plan to answer 'not covered' honestly for the vehicles you cannot price
a price source with enough freshness to quote at auction time, and a stated tolerance for how stale is too stale
labour-cost assumptions per region, since the repair estimate and therefore the Total Loss verdict depend on them even though the page never names them
a review path for the regulatory vocabulary: cite the standards and thresholds you invoke, or drop the claims that read like compliance approval
clone_cost.estimate: 5-7 weeks for a single-jurisdiction version a buyer would trust; a year of data work for the catalog that makes it worth using
clone_cost.why: The application is ordinary: photo preprocessing with Sharp, a queue on Inngest, Prisma over Postgres, Next.js and Stripe, and a multimodal model call with search grounding for part numbers and live prices - two or three weeks for someone fluent in that stack. The time goes into the parts catalog and the pricing source, which are the only defensible parts of the product and are not built here at all: structuring OEM data per make, model and year, keeping prices from becoming stale, and deciding what to return when coverage is thin. Adding a second jurisdiction (ECE instead of DOT/SAE, EUR, per-country import and inspection rules) is a further multiplier rather than a config flag. A clone can reproduce the flow quickly; it cannot reproduce the asset.

audit.what_to_steal: Publish the decision rule, not just the score: the Loss Ratio names both inputs, states the band edges, and returns a verdict - a reader can recompute it and argue with it, which is more than most 'AI estimate' products offer. Then steal the failure-surface design: scarcity detection wired to an advisory banner, with the explicit principle that admitting no coverage beats a confident wrong answer. Region should be an input, not a translation - standards family, currency and title/import/emissions/inspection rules change what the estimate means, so carry them through the model call and the UI together. Free adjacent utility as acquisition: a VIN-to-window-sticker generator that costs nothing to run and lands the same audience on the paid product. And three model tiers with automatic failover in a flow running against an auction clock.
audit.what_breaks_first: Catalog coverage, on both ends of the pipeline. The 700,000-row figure is spread over 60-plus makes and their model years, so the first user with a twelve-year-old European hatchback gets either no parts or a plausible wrong code - and the scarcity banner only helps if scarcity is detected against coverage the product actually measures rather than against a lookup that happens to miss. Second, the severity-to-cost link: the bands assume the repair estimate is close enough to divide by resale value, and near 40 and 70 percent a modest error in labour or parts changes 'repairable' into 'Total Loss' with no stated error model to tell the buyer which side of the line they are on. Third, spatial normalisation: the driver-side versus passenger-side disambiguation is the difference between quoting a mirror or a fender, and a cropped, low-light auction photo is precisely where a 3D-normalisation step degrades.

prior_art.relation: both turn a stream of sensor evidence into a regulatory-flavoured verdict for a human to act on, and neither page publishes an accuracy figure - the fisheries tool goes further and states there is no ground truth for its risk classification, while Carbender's page implies its bands come from external standards without naming them. Read together, they are the two failure modes of the same design: admit the measurement problem, or borrow authority from a regulator.

both end in an artifact a person checks rather than an action the system takes - a repair plan PDF against a cited diff - and both leave the accuracy of the underlying judgement unmeasured. The difference is what they attach evidence to: Continuity grounds a claim against the live web and shows the citation next to the verdict, while Carbender grounds a part number against a proprietary catalog the reader cannot inspect, so its traceability stops at the vendor boundary.

both put a machine-readable judgement in front of a purchase decision and both monetise through the transaction surface rather than the model; the marketplace tool's advantage is that its output is checked by the market on the next listing, whereas a repair estimate is only checked when the parts arrive, so the feedback loop is months long.

hazard.note: This is a money decision dressed in regulatory vocabulary. The product returns a Total Loss verdict and a repair estimate that a buyer may bid against, while invoking DOT, SAE and ECE standards, country-specific import, title, emissions and inspection requirements, and a Loss Ratio band policy described as 'matching EU & US salvage threshold standards' with no citation and no named issuing body for either threshold. Nothing on the page states who is liable when the estimate is wrong, no accuracy figure exists for either the part identification or the price, and the resale denominator comes from another estimate rather than a transaction record, so a High-band verdict near a boundary can flip on inputs that are both soft. The team's stated posture is the right instinct - a wrong OEM code shown with false confidence is worse than no result - but an interface banner is not a compliance sign-off, and a tool that names regulators should either cite them or stop invoking them. Held from promotion on that basis: publishable as a documented case, not as a usable figure.
